notable_claims: The University of Toronto declined to intercept or censor violent pornographic material on the Internet.
Congressional candidates in California's 14th District committed to protecting constitutional liberties against technological threats.
University of Illinois implemented an interim e-mail advisory addressing privacy and access to electronic files.
classification.summary: This digest abstract summarizes key discussions regarding university computer policies, including email privacy at the University of Illinois and network policies at Rice University. It covers early debates on Usenet censorship (specifically adult content), anonymous posting in academic settings, and political commitments to protect technology-related civil liberties.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.33

notable_claims: Electronic files of State of Illinois employees are considered public documents under the Illinois Freedom of Information Act.
Confidentiality of electronic media cannot be guaranteed due to routine maintenance or system administration.
classification.summary: The University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign issued an interim electronic mail advisory regarding the privacy of files on electronic media. The policy warns users that confidentiality cannot be guaranteed due to system administration and notes that electronic files are subject to the Illinois Freedom of Information Act.
classification.title: New U. of Illinois (and NCSA) Computer Privacy policy

identity.subject: Article 1--New U. of Illinois (and NCSA) Computer Privacy policy

notable_claims: Rice University's Owlnet established a Student Advisory Committee to propose policies and act as a disciplinary body.
System administrators at Rice adopted a formal Statement of Ethics regarding user privacy and confidentiality.
Previous university policy required Vice President for Information Systems permission for students to send communications off-campus.
Critics argued that selectively enforced, vague policies could be used as weapons against 'troublemakers'.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie shares updated computing policies from Owlnet at Rice University, provided by Joseph A. Watters. The documents highlight a student-led advisory committee for policy and discipline, as well as a System Administrator Statement of Ethics regarding privacy. The item also includes critiques of previous 'authoritarian' policies that required explicit permission for off-campus electronic communication.
classification.title: Article 2--Rice U. - Overview

notable_claims: The University of Toronto declined to intercept or censor Internet files containing violent pornography.
The University of Manitoba cut off access to a 'sex-bondage' file following complaints and police visits.
David Sadleir (U of T) argued that if a recipient must actively select information, there is no need for university intervention.
John Drake (ONet) claimed the network is a carrier, not a provider or publisher, and should not decide which material is proper to transmit.
classification.summary: A report on the University of Toronto's refusal to censor pornographic material on the Internet, contrasting its stance with the University of Manitoba's decision to block a 'sex-bondage' file. U of T officials argued that active user selection removes the need for censorship and that blocking institutions would restrict access to useful information. The article also highlights ONet's position as a carrier rather than a publisher of information.
classification.title: Network Pornography Elicits Little Reaction at U of T

notable_claims: The court found that artistic expression is at the core of a democratic society's cultural and political vitality, comparable to academic speech.
classification.summary: A federal judge ruled that the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) 'decency clause' was unconstitutional due to being too vague and overbroad. The ruling emphasized that artistic expression is as central to a democratic society as academic speech or journalism. This followed a legal challenge by four artists whose grants were denied based on political content.
classification.title: Federal judge rules NEA decency clause unconstitutional

identity.subject: Article 5--[UPI] Federal judge rules NEA decency clause unconstitutional

notable_claims: This is believed to be the first time major-party congressional candidates committed to explicit action to protect technology-related civil liberties.
classification.summary: Jim Warren reports that several congressional candidates in California's 14th District signed formal commitments to protect 'Electronic Civil Liberties.' The commitment, stemming from the First Conference on Computers, Freedom & Privacy (1991), sought to ensure constitutional protections for speech, press, and search and seizure applied to electronic media. It included a proposed constitutional amendment by Professor Laurence H. Tribe.
classification.title: Major Congressional Candidates Commit to Elec. Civil Liberties

identity.subject: Article 6--File 3--Major Congressional Candidates Commit to Elec. Civil Liberties

notable_claims: Private machine owners are not legally required to propagate potentially offensive messages.
Direct email is distinct from broadcast newsgroups, placing more responsibility on the sender for offensive content.
classification.summary: Jamie Gritton responds to Grady Ward's guidelines for system managers regarding freedom of speech and offensive content. Gritton argues that private machine owners are not legally forced to propagate offensive messages and suggests different management strategies for newsgroups versus direct email. The exchange highlights early debates over the responsibilities of system administrators in moderating network communication.
classification.title: Article 8--Re: standard managers reply

notable_claims: Repeated unwanted email can constitute harassment.
Harassment by computer is legally considered harassment.
Public newsgroup articles that offend a user are generally not classified as harassment.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides advice on dealing with computer-based harassment, distinguishing between private unwanted communications and public newsgroup posts. He suggests documenting the harassment, notifying administrators, and using email filters. The post references legal precedents and EFF resources regarding censorship and harassment.
classification.title: Article 9--Re: vax harrassment

notable_claims: Anonymous posting services for PLATO notesfiles met requirements for student anonymity by the end of the 1970s.
Students may avoid asking questions due to fear of peer or instructor judgment, making anonymous channels a significant pedagogical aid.
classification.summary: Douglas W. Jones argues for the necessity of controlled anonymous communication tools in academic settings to encourage student participation and questioning without fear of judgment. He discusses the technical challenges of trust in anonymous mail servers and suggests moderated newsgroups as a potential solution. He references the PLATO project at the University of Illinois as an early successful implementation of these features in the 1970s.
classification.title: Article 10--Anonymous postings
